risks.risk: Extreme single-service-line revenue concentration - IT staffing is stated to be approximately 98% of revenue
risks.note: The MD&A states this reflects the Company's specialist positioning but means a downturn in enterprise tech hiring could significantly impact the Company. Management's stated mitigation is to diversify revenue across managed services, statement of work and learning solutions - i.e. the diversification is an intent, not yet a fact. The IT staffing business is separately confirmed as the principal revenue contributor at approximately 98% of total revenue for the year.

risks.risk: Cyclicality of enterprise tech hiring and dependence on global tech spending
risks.note: Staffing demand is tied to enterprise confidence and global tech spending. The AR flags that Q4 FY 2025-26 IT staffing growth slowed to 0.2% (from 12.3% YoY in Q1), which it presents as evidence of high quarterly volatility even in a strong year - the full-year growth figure reflects early gains consolidated rather than extended in the second half.

risks.risk: Competitive intensity and bill-rate pricing pressure against a thin net margin
risks.note: Formalisation shifts volume to organised providers and intensifies competition for mandates. The AR explicitly states the thin net margin means slight bill-rate reductions or higher bench costs disproportionately impact profitability. Pricing competition as players formalise the market is named as a key factor for the coming year.

risks.risk: Labour-code transition: wage and gratuity cost inflation that cannot always be passed through
risks.note: The four labour codes (effective 21 November 2025) target parity between fixed-term and permanent employees on wages and benefits, with gratuity after one year of service. Central and state rules are stated to be pending notification. The AR flags wage and gratuity cost inflation as a margin risk because it cannot always be passed through in bill rates, and notes compliance obligations will keep evolving during the transition. The same codes are also framed as an opportunity favouring organised, audited providers.

risks.risk: Client concentration combined with receivables and working-capital risk
risks.note: Staffing businesses incur wage costs before collecting payment, making the working-capital cycle sensitive to payment delays or defaults by major clients, which the AR states could harm liquidity and profitability. 'Client concentration and competitive pricing' is separately repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.

risks.risk: Cybersecurity and data-privacy exposure across recruitment and payroll systems
risks.note: Digital recruitment platforms and payroll systems hold large amounts of personal data; breaches could lead to regulatory, contractual and reputational damage. The AR notes client due diligence on information security is now standard in evaluations, so this is a commercial gating item as well as a loss risk. 'Information security and protection of employee and client data' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.

risks.risk: Deployable-skills shortage rather than candidate shortage
risks.note: Talent shortages in specialised skills (AI, cloud, data, security) stem from deployability constraints, not availability. This limits converting mandates into billed deployments and drives up associate pay - a direct constraint on both revenue conversion and gross margin. 'Dependence on availability of qualified talent' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.

risks.risk: Rapid technological change requiring continuous investment in assessment, training, certification and sourcing platforms
risks.note: Skill-demand shifts are stated to move faster than traditional training cycles, requiring ongoing investment simply to stay deployable. 'Rapid technological changes in recruitment and workforce management' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.

risks.risk: Macroeconomic conditions affecting client hiring plans, and regulatory/statutory compliance burden
risks.note: Both are named in the MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' major-risk list. The Company states it has established appropriate internal processes and compliance mechanisms to identify, monitor and mitigate these risks, and that internal control systems commensurate with the size and nature of the business are in place, with the internal audit function periodically reviewing effectiveness and significant observations plus corrective actions presented to the Audit Committee.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- GCC ecosystem build-out in India is the primary stated demand driver: the AR states India now hosts over 2,100 GCCs employing more than 2.3 million professionals, with industry estimates projecting the ecosystem to cross USD 98 billion in revenue by the end of FY 2025-26
- Around 60% of new roles being created within GCCs are stated to be in AI, data and platform skills - described as precisely the areas where DTL has been building its delivery muscle
- Policy tailwind: the Union Budget for FY 2026-27 is stated to have strengthened the GCC runway through a unified safe-harbour margin for IT services and an extended tax holiday for foreign cloud providers operating in India
- Organised staffing formalisation: the industry added approximately 1.18 lakh formal flexi workers in FY 2025-26, taking the ISF-member workforce to about 1.91 million, an increase of close to 8% year-on-year
- IT staffing outgrew general staffing in FY26 - new employment growth of 10.1% YoY versus 7.9% for general staffing - described as a clear return to growth after a subdued preceding cycle
- Demand is concentrated in a specific client cohort rather than a broad recovery: GCCs made up 73% of new IT hires, mainly in AI, machine learning, cloud, cybersecurity and data engineering, while traditional IT services hiring stayed subdued
- Cyclical caution flagged: momentum was uneven, with IT staffing at 5.5% QoQ and 12.3% YoY in Q1 FY26 slowing to 0.2% growth by Q4 - the full-year figure reflects early gains consolidated rather than extended in the second half
- Market size context: in FY 2023-24 the Indian IT flexi staffing market was valued at USD 4.9 billion with around 597,000 professionals, projected to grow at a 7% CAGR through FY 2025-26; India is described as the second-largest IT flexi staffing market in South Asia-Pacific
- The binding constraint is stated to be deployable, current skills rather than candidate availability - shifting the staffing focus from sourcing to capability building, assessment, training, certification and bench management, which in turn influences fill and bill rates
- Geographic dispersion of demand beyond traditional corridors into Ahmedabad, Coimbatore, Visakhapatnam, Surat, Kochi and Nagpur, requiring broader sourcing, compliance and payroll infrastructure - favouring providers who build it
- Labour codes (four codes, implementation from November 2025) raise compliance standards and costs, stated to favour scaled compliant providers while squeezing margins for those unable to pass costs through
- Company-level operating leverage drivers cited by the Chairperson: scaling of the Managed Services business, traction of SOW and outcome-based delivery models with enterprise clients, and AI-led recruitment/delivery processes now embedded in day-to-day operations
- Ushta Te performed ahead of budget in its first full year within the DTL fold, with acquisition synergies stated to be beginning to flow through in both revenue and operational efficiency
- Headcount scaled from around 740 to over 2,000 professionals in twelve months and the enterprise client base grew from 24 to over 65 marquee names
- Macro backdrop: India expanded 7.7% in real terms in FY2025-26 with FY2026-27 growth projected at about 6.5-6.6%, against global growth slowing to approximately 3.0% in 2026
- Longer-horizon opportunity: India's gig workforce is expected to grow from 77 lakhs in 2020-21 to 2.35 crore by 2029-30, with labour codes integrating gig workers into social security frameworks
- Watch items management names for the year ahead: state-level rule updates under the labour codes, wage inflation and pass-through effects, indirect tax treatment of manpower services, global tech spending trends affecting GCC hiring, and pricing competition as players formalise the market

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Strengthen the Company's leadership position in the GCC and technology staffing ecosystem - the Chairperson describes the Global Capability Centre segment as 'the strategic backbone of DTL'
- Position DTL not merely as a staffing provider to GCCs but as a long-term delivery partner across their India build-out - skilled talent at scale, managed services and increasingly outcome-based solutions
- Grow managed services and SOW-led (statement-of-work) revenue as a share of total business, with outcome-based revenue expected to grow disproportionately
- Continue to improve margins, cash flows and return on capital
- Invest in technology, AI and the leadership bench required to support scale
- Deepen relationships with existing clients while expanding into new marquee accounts
- Pursue disciplined and profitable growth, both organic and inorganic
- Expand the tier-2 city delivery footprint as part of the FY27 roadmap
- Formalise the existing AI-led recruitment and delivery workflows into an AI Implementation Charter with clear rollout milestones for FY 2026-27
- Complete and extract synergies from the Ushta Te Consultancy Services LLP integration, which management states is adding scale, marquee client access and delivery bandwidth
- No dividend policy figures are disclosed in the routed governance sections; the stance has to be read off the Board's Report and the Chairperson's message [PROVENANCE: both from the sibling profile / strategy_outlook bundles]. The Board does not recommend any dividend on the equity shares for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, and no amount was transferred to the General Reserve during the year - both stated nils, i.e. full retention. The Company did not accept any deposits within the meaning of Sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013 during the year, and no principal or interest on deposits was outstanding as at March 31, 2026. The stated reinvestment intent is growth-led: the Board approved a proposed preferential issue of up to 3,98,800 fully convertible warrants at ₹115 per warrant (aggregating approximately ₹4.58 crore), subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals and stated to be fully subscribed by promoters, directors, key managerial personnel and senior leadership, with proceeds intended to support repayment of certain borrowings, strengthening of the balance sheet and continued investment in growth, technology and AI capabilities alongside future strategic opportunities. Stated strategic-priority framing is to continue improving margins, cash flows and return on capital and to pursue disciplined and profitable growth, both organic and inorganic. Governance context: the equity shares are listed on the NSE Emerge platform, so by virtue of Regulation 15(2)(b) of SEBI LODR the corporate-governance provisions specified therein are not applicable to the extent of the SME-exchange exemption, though the Company states it endeavours to follow sound corporate-governance practices and the Companies Act, 2013 requirements continue to apply. The Board met seven times in FY 2025-26 with no change in Board constitution during the year; the Audit Committee met four times (12-05-2025, 12-08-2025, 12-11-2025, 06-02-2026) with 100% attendance at each, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee once (16-05-2025, 100% attendance), and the Stakeholders' Relationship Committee once (25-03-2026, 100% attendance); a separate meeting of Independent Directors was held on March 25, 2026 attended by all Independent Directors. NOTE ON PROMOTERS: no shareholding pattern, no holding/ultimate-holding company disclosure and no 'promoter director' labelling appears anywhere in the routed text, so the promoters list is honestly empty; the only promoter reference in the whole bundle set is the Chairperson's statement that the warrant issue was 'fully subscribed by promoters, directors, key managerial personnel, and senior leadership, including myself', which names no one. The three Form AOC-2 counterparties (Jk Technosoft Limited, Jk Education Foundation, Jaykay Enterprises Ltd) point to a JK/Jaykay group linkage through KMP significant influence, but the AR does not state that any of them is a promoter entity. NOTE ON ESOP: the Corporate Governance Report extract is truncated at the heading 'EMPLOYEES' STOCK', so any employee stock option disclosure was not delivered.
- No BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report) section was supplied in the routed text, and no environmental, emissions, energy or water disclosure appears anywhere in this bundle - so there is no ESG TARGET to report. What follows are the only material, evidenced ESG-relevant facts the routed text supports.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion is treated as a commercial as well as a social item: the MD&A states diversity commitments are now part of client evaluation, serving as a competitive edge and expanding the talent pool, and that female participation in IT flexi staffing averages about 37%, well above the national female labour-force rate. DEI initiatives are separately listed as an area of continued investment under Human Resources. NOTE: the 37% figure is an INDUSTRY statistic, not a disclosed DTL workforce number - the AR gives no DTL-specific gender split.
- Social impact through workforce formalisation is the Company's core stated ESG linkage: under the employer-of-record model the Company carries wages, benefits and statutory compliance, and the MD&A frames the staffing industry's contribution as turning undocumented work into jobs with payslips, provident fund, insurance and employment records.
- Human-capital investment areas stated under Human Resources: employee training and skill development, leadership development initiatives, compliance and workplace safety awareness, employee engagement programmes, diversity/equity/inclusion initiatives, and performance management and career development. Industrial relations are stated to have remained cordial throughout the year. As on March 31, 2026 the Company states it maintained a diverse and competent workforce of experienced professionals and young talent (no headcount or diversity numbers given in this section).
- Learning and development is stated to serve a dual role - a revenue stream and a route to convert candidates into deployable staffing supply - against a backdrop where few in India hold formal vocational or technical certification and about a quarter of 15-29 year-olds are not in employment, education or training.
- Quality management certification: ISO 9001:2015 Certificate of Conformance issued by Global Enterprise for Excellence (India) under licence from Global Enterprise for Excellence Limited, UK; Certificate Number 06261101060; Original Issue Date 11.06.2026; Last Audit Completion Date 05.06.2026; Valid Till 04.06.2029. Scope spans HR Solutions & Services, Payroll Management, Contingent Staffing Services, Permanent Manpower Solutions, Corporate Training, Learning Solutions & Digital Content Solutions, Software Solutions & Services, Engineering Solutions & IT/Infrastructure Services, Consulting Services and Outsourced projects including Content & Technical Writing, and Business Process Management & Managed Services. [PROVENANCE: this certificate arrived inside the risks_esg bundle's own '=== CORPORATE OVERVIEW ===' block; it is also carried in the profile bundle and is recorded in profile.json under certifications.]
- Governance framing carried in this bundle's Corporate Overview: the Company states it maintains a governance framework promoting transparency, accountability, regulatory compliance and effective risk management, designed to safeguard stakeholder interests - boilerplate, and the sentence is truncated mid-word ('supporting sustainable busine').
- STATED ABSENCE / GAP: no CSR disclosure, no environmental metric, no emissions or energy target, no supply-chain or human-rights policy, no whistleblower/POSH disclosure and no ESG rating appears in the routed sections. This is absence of delivered text (the bundle contains no BRSR and the MD&A is truncated at both ends), not a disclosed nil.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: DTL is an asset-light IT staffing and managed-services business: the routed sections disclose no plants, no production capacity and no physical commissioning/ramp projects. Expansion in this AR is expressed as entity, footprint and capability build-out rather than plant capex. (a) Inorganic footprint: the Company acquired a 99.99% ownership interest in Ushta Te Consultancy Services LLP with effect from May 12, 2025, and subscribed to/acquired 100% of the equity interest in Diensten Tech Inc., incorporated in the State of Wyoming, USA, with effect from November 10, 2025, making it a wholly owned foreign subsidiary - stated to be part of a strategy to broaden service capabilities, expand the client base and establish an international presence. It also entered a Business Transfer Agreement dated October 01, 2025 with Klaus IT Solutions Private Limited for the phased transfer/novation of specified client contracts and the corresponding employees (expressly NOT a share acquisition). [PROVENANCE: sibling profile bundle.] (c) Forward footprint intent: the Chairperson's FY27 roadmap states the tier-2 city delivery footprint expands and that managed services and outcome-based revenue grow disproportionately; the intent is also to formalise AI-led workflows into an AI Implementation Charter with clear rollout milestones for FY 2026-27. [PROVENANCE: sibling strategy_outlook/profile bundle - the Chairperson extract inside the capex bundle is truncated before the 'LOOKING AHEAD' section.] (d) Industry-level (NOT company) expansion commentary supplied in this bundle: IT flexi staffing demand is dispersing beyond traditional corridors into Ahmedabad, Coimbatore, Visakhapatnam, Surat, Kochi and Nagpur, and the MD&A notes latent demand addressable through geographic expansion into tier-II and tier-III markets - this is market commentary, not a stated DTL site plan. moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Employer-of-record model in which the Company carries wages, benefits and statutory compliance while the client directs the worker - the AR states that scale, compliance and financial strength, rather than recruitment reach, are the main entry barriers in organised staffing
- Stated 50+ years of cumulative leadership team industry experience
- On-rolls employee strength stated as 2,000+ (2,037 employees vs 741 in FY25), giving deployable delivery bandwidth
- Client logos stated to have grown to 65 from 24, described in the Chairperson's message as marquee enterprise names
- ISO 9001:2015 certified across HR, payroll, staffing, training, software, engineering/IT-infrastructure and managed-services scope
- Multi-location delivery footprint - Delhi headquarters with branches across five Indian states plus a USA office
- Specialist positioning in IT/GCC staffing rather than volume general staffing, which the AR links to longer deployments, higher bill rates and lower churn

- Inorganic capability additions during the year - a 99.99% interest in Ushta Te Consultancy Services LLP and a wholly owned US subsidiary, Diensten Tech Inc.

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Extreme single-service-line revenue concentration - IT staffing is stated to be approximately 98% of revenue — The MD&A states this reflects the Company's specialist positioning but means a downturn in enterprise tech hiring could significantly impact the Company. Management's stated mitigation is to diversify revenue across managed services, statement of work and learning solutions - i.e. the diversification is an intent, not yet a fact. The IT staffing business is separately confirmed as the principal revenue contributor at approximately 98% of total revenue for the year.
- Cyclicality of enterprise tech hiring and dependence on global tech spending — Staffing demand is tied to enterprise confidence and global tech spending. The AR flags that Q4 FY 2025-26 IT staffing growth slowed to 0.2% (from 12.3% YoY in Q1), which it presents as evidence of high quarterly volatility even in a strong year - the full-year growth figure reflects early gains consolidated rather than extended in the second half.
- Competitive intensity and bill-rate pricing pressure against a thin net margin — Formalisation shifts volume to organised providers and intensifies competition for mandates. The AR explicitly states the thin net margin means slight bill-rate reductions or higher bench costs disproportionately impact profitability. Pricing competition as players formalise the market is named as a key factor for the coming year.
- Labour-code transition: wage and gratuity cost inflation that cannot always be passed through — The four labour codes (effective 21 November 2025) target parity between fixed-term and permanent employees on wages and benefits, with gratuity after one year of service. Central and state rules are stated to be pending notification. The AR flags wage and gratuity cost inflation as a margin risk because it cannot always be passed through in bill rates, and notes compliance obligations will keep evolving during the transition. The same codes are also framed as an opportunity favouring organised, audited providers.
- Client concentration combined with receivables and working-capital risk — Staffing businesses incur wage costs before collecting payment, making the working-capital cycle sensitive to payment delays or defaults by major clients, which the AR states could harm liquidity and profitability. 'Client concentration and competitive pricing' is separately repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.
- Cybersecurity and data-privacy exposure across recruitment and payroll systems — Digital recruitment platforms and payroll systems hold large amounts of personal data; breaches could lead to regulatory, contractual and reputational damage. The AR notes client due diligence on information security is now standard in evaluations, so this is a commercial gating item as well as a loss risk. 'Information security and protection of employee and client data' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.
- Deployable-skills shortage rather than candidate shortage — Talent shortages in specialised skills (AI, cloud, data, security) stem from deployability constraints, not availability. This limits converting mandates into billed deployments and drives up associate pay - a direct constraint on both revenue conversion and gross margin. 'Dependence on availability of qualified talent' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.
- Rapid technological change requiring continuous investment in assessment, training, certification and sourcing platforms — Skill-demand shifts are stated to move faster than traditional training cycles, requiring ongoing investment simply to stay deployable. 'Rapid technological changes in recruitment and workforce management' is repeated in the Risks and Concerns list.
- Macroeconomic conditions affecting client hiring plans, and regulatory/statutory compliance burden — Both are named in the MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' major-risk list. The Company states it has established appropriate internal processes and compliance mechanisms to identify, monitor and mitigate these risks, and that internal control systems commensurate with the size and nature of the business are in place, with the internal audit function periodically reviewing effectiveness and significant observations plus corrective actions presented to the Audit Committee.
